subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 19-year-old woman presents with 1 week of dysuria and a mild mucopurulent vaginal discharge. She is sexually active with a new partner and denies fever. Nucleic acid amplification testing returns positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Her partner has no symptoms but also tests positive.
question: Which of the following is the best first-line treatment for this patient, assuming she is not pregnant?
explanation_correct: Chlamydial infection is treated with doxycycline, and azithromycin is used for pregnant patients. Ceftriaxone is added if concurrent gonorrhea testing is positive, since coinfection is common. Beta-lactams such as penicillin and amoxicillin are ineffective because the chlamydial cell wall lacks classic peptidoglycan due to reduced muramic acid.

explanation_incorrect.A: Penicillin G is the treatment for syphilis and is not effective against Chlamydia.
explanation_incorrect.B: TMP-SMX is used for Nocardia and as an alternative in macrolide-allergic pertussis, not for chlamydial urethritis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amoxicillin is a beta-lactam and is not the recommended chlamydial therapy, related to the organism's atypical cell wall.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ceftriaxone is for gonorrhea and is added only if gonococcal coinfection is documented or not excluded.

educationalObjective: Uncomplicated chlamydial infection is treated with doxycycline, using azithromycin in pregnancy and adding ceftriaxone only if gonorrhea is also present.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 26-year-old man presents with a small, painless ulcer on the penis and a 5-day history of tender swelling of the right groin. Examination shows indurated, matted inguinal lymph nodes, one of which is fluctuant. He denies systemic symptoms. Infection with serotypes L1 to L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis is confirmed.
question: Which of the following best describes this presentation?

options.text: Primary syphilis, with a painless chancre and nontender bilateral lymphadenopathy
Chancroid, with a painful ragged ulcer and suppurative nodes from Haemophilus ducreyi
Genital herpes, with grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base
Trachoma from serotypes A, B, and C with follicular conjunctivitis
Lymphogranuloma venereum, with a small painless ulcer progressing to painful ulcerating inguinal buboes

explanation_correct: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes L1, L2, and L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum, which starts with small painless genital ulcers and progresses to swollen, painful inguinal lymph nodes that ulcerate as buboes. It is treated with doxycycline. The distinction from other causes of genital ulceration rests on the painless initial ulcer with markedly tender, suppurating nodes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary syphilis usually produces nontender inguinal adenopathy, and the nodes are not fluctuant buboes; serologic confirmation would be positive for T pallidum.
explanation_incorrect.B: Chancroid produces a painful, ragged ulcer with purulent exudate, whereas the LGV ulcer here is small and painless.
explanation_incorrect.C: Herpetic lesions are painful grouped vesicles, not a single painless ulcer with unilateral inguinal buboes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Serotypes A, B, and C cause chronic follicular conjunctivitis and blindness in resource-limited settings, not genital ulcer disease.

educationalObjective: Genital serotypes L1 to L3 of C trachomatis cause lymphogranuloma venereum, a painless genital ulcer followed by painful ulcerating inguinal buboes treated with doxycycline.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: An 8-day-old infant born by vaginal delivery to an untreated mother presents with bilateral eye discharge and swelling of the eyelids. Examination shows purulent conjunctivitis with redness and edema of the conjunctivae. The infant has no fever and is feeding well. The mother had no prenatal care.
question: Which of the following organisms most likely causes conjunctivitis in this infant, and which form is responsible for infecting the conjunctival cells?

options.text: Chlamydia trachomatis, with the reticulate body entering host cells
Chlamydia trachomatis, with the elementary body entering host cells
Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with the pillated form entering host cells
Haemophilus influenzae, with the capsular type b polysaccharide entering cells
Staphylococcus aureus, with the exfoliative toxin entering the conjunctiva

explanation_correct: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D through K cause neonatal conjunctivitis at 1 to 2 weeks after birth, later than the 2 to 5 day onset of gonococcal conjunctivitis. Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular organisms that cannot make their own ATP; the small, dense elementary body is the infectious form that enters the cell by endocytosis, and it then transforms into the replicating reticulate body. Inclusion bodies containing reticulate bodies can be seen on Giemsa or fluorescent antibody stained smears.

explanation_incorrect.A: The replicating reticulate body is the intracellular form; the infectious particle that enters cells is the elementary body.
explanation_incorrect.C: Gonococcal conjunctivitis presents earlier, typically 2 to 5 days after birth, with a hyperacute purulent discharge, and prevention is by erythromycin eye ointment.
explanation_incorrect.D: Haemophilus causes conjunctivitis and otitis media in older children, but the 1 to 2 week timing and afebrile infant point to chlamydia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Staphylococcal conjunctivitis is common in neonates but is not associated with a latency of 1 to 2 weeks or with the intracellular life cycle described.

educationalObjective: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis appears 1 to 2 weeks after delivery and is caused by the infectious elementary body, which becomes the replicating reticulate body inside the cell.
